title: Recover the Original Array
statement:
Someone started from an array `arr` of `n` positive integers and a positive integer `k`. From every element they produced two numbers, `arr[i] - k` and `arr[i] + k`, then threw all `2n` of these numbers together without remembering which element or which side each came from. You receive them, in some order, as `nums`.

Return an array `arr` of `n` integers that could have produced `nums`: there must be a positive integer `k` such that the `2n` values `arr[i] - k` and `arr[i] + k` are exactly the values of `nums`, counting repeats. At least one such array is guaranteed to exist. When several arrays work, any of them is accepted, and its elements may be in any order.
constraints: At least one valid arr exists
notes:
## Intuition

Once `k` is known, recovering `arr` is easy, so the work is finding `k`. The smallest value of `nums` can only be a "minus k" value (its "plus k" partner would be even smaller), and its partner is that value plus `2k`, which is some other element of `nums`. So enumerating the other elements gives at most `2n - 1` candidate gaps `2k`; only positive even gaps count.

For one candidate gap, sort the values and pair greedily: the smallest unpaired value must also be a "minus k" value, so it must be matched with an unpaired copy of itself plus the gap. If that copy is missing the gap is wrong. (Trying every split of `nums` into two halves also works, but it is exponential.)

## Approach

1. Sort `nums`; `n` is half its length.
2. For each `j`, let `gap = nums[j] - nums[0]`. Skip it if it is zero, odd, or the same as the previous `j`'s gap.
3. Pair values with two pointers: `low` walks over the unpaired values in order; `high` moves forward (it never needs to go back, because targets only grow) to the first unpaired value at least `nums[low] + gap`.
4. If that value is not exactly `nums[low] + gap`, this gap fails. Otherwise mark `high` as used and push the midpoint `nums[low] + gap / 2` to `arr`.
5. When all `n` pairs are found, return `arr`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted `nums = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]`. With `j = 1`, `gap = 2`. `low = 0` (2) pairs with 4, giving 3; `low = 2` (6) pairs with 8, giving 7; `low = 4` (10) pairs with 12, giving 11. Three pairs, so `[3, 7, 11]` is returned (`k = 1`).

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): up to `2n` candidate gaps, each checked in O(n) by the two pointers, after an O(n log n) sort.
- Space: O(n) for `used` and `arr`.

## Pitfalls

- `k` must be positive: a zero gap (equal values) is never a valid candidate.
- An odd gap cannot be `2k` for an integer `k`.
- Each value can be used once: a value already taken as a partner must be skipped by both pointers.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of the original array |
| `j` | index of the candidate partner of the smallest value |
| `gap` | the candidate `2k` |
| `used` | marks values already taken as partners |
| `low`, `high` | the smaller value of a pair and the search for its partner |
| `arr` | the recovered elements for the current gap |

narration.2: Sort the values so the smallest unpaired value is always the next one to the right.
narration.3: The original array has half as many elements as nums.
narration.5: Enumerate the partner of the smallest value; each choice fixes a candidate gap of 2k.
narration.6: The candidate gap between the smallest value and this partner.
narration.7: k must be a positive integer, so the gap must be positive and even; a repeated value gives a gap already tried.
narration.10: Start a fresh pairing for this gap: nothing is used yet.
narration.13: Walk over the values from smallest to largest.
narration.14: A value already taken as someone's partner is skipped.
narration.17: The partner lies to the right of low, and never left of where the previous search stopped.
narration.18: Move high past used values and values too small to be the partner.
narration.21: The first candidate is not exactly nums[low] + gap, so this gap cannot pair everything.
narration.24: Take that value as the partner of nums[low].
narration.25: The original element sits halfway between the pair.
narration.28: ...so this array is a valid answer.
